# How the model will likely be used {#sec-forward}

This section is informed speculation. Nothing in it is a result of this paper.

## Every number in this series is measured at the wrong price

Paper 4 asked whether the model adds anything given a market price. Two
answers came back.

Against the **settled starting price** it adds nothing that can be
distinguished from zero. The pooled model-probability coefficient in a
two-stage conditional logit was 0.068 for the paper-2b ranking model and 0.039
for the gradient-boosted trees over 2,182 races, with 95% intervals reaching
no higher than 0.204.

Against the **overnight racecard forecast price** it adds a great deal: 1.037
and 1.026 on the earlier test half, 0.746 and 0.723 on the later.

So the model knows something the overnight price does not and nothing the
settled price does not. Its value sits in the hours between those two moments.
Every backtest in papers 1 to 6 settles at the closing end of that interval,
which is the one price where the model was already known to add nothing.

That reframes @sec-found. The searches were not failing to find a good rule.
They were looking for a rule strong enough to beat a margin at a price where
the model has no informational advantage left.

## The likely use is a price trade, not a winner-picking trade

Backing at the off means picking winners against a market that has already
absorbed everything the model knows. Backing early means taking a price the
model thinks is too long, which is a different bet with a different payoff.

The trade has two exits. Hold to the result and collect at the early price if
the horse wins. Or lay the same horse back on the exchange once the price
shortens, taking the difference and carrying no result risk at all. The second
exit is available whether or not the horse runs well, which is the point: the
bet is on the price moving, not on the horse.

The mechanism this leans on is convergence. Early markets are thin and
dominated by bookmaker prices and money that has not looked closely. As race
time approaches, liquidity builds and prices move toward fair value. A model
that approximates the closing price from pre-race information alone identifies
horses whose early price has not yet moved. The edge, if it exists, is in
front-running that convergence.

Paper 4's numbers are consistent with that and do not establish it. What they
establish is where to look.

## The metric changes with the trade

Judge it by closing line value, not ROI. Did the price taken beat the price at
the off?

That is a per-bet measurement rather than a per-win one. It is available on
every bet, it does not wait for a result, and it converges in hundreds of bets
rather than tens of thousands. ROI on a win market converges slowly because
almost all its variance sits in whether a few long-priced bets landed. The
field-size rule's entire 75-point reversal in @sec-found is 42 winners
becoming 19.

This is the reason every ROI interval in this series is too wide to read. The
intervals in @sec-found run 20 to 50 points wide on samples of 300 to 1,000
bets. A metric that resolves in hundreds of bets is not a refinement here. It
is the difference between being able to tell whether the strategy works and
not being able to tell.

If the convergence thesis is right, closing line value is positive and shows
up quickly. If it is wrong, that shows up quickly too, and long before an ROI
would say anything.

## The exchange changes the arithmetic

Bookmaker prices carry the over-round in @sec-searched: from
`r p6_fpct(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size == 4] / 100, 1)`
at four runners to
`r p6_fpct(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size == 14] / 100, 1)`
at fourteen. Field sizes 8 to 12 hold
`r p6_fpct(sum(p6_overround_val$n_races[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / p6_universe$n_val_races, 0)`
of the search races and pay between
`r p6_fpct(min(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / 100, 1)`
and
`r p6_fpct(max(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / 100, 1)`.

An exchange charges commission on net winnings instead, typically 2 to 5%.
That gap is larger than any effect this paper searched for. The best
test-split return in the whole shortlist is
`r p6_fpct(max(p6_round3_test$roi, na.rm = TRUE), 1, TRUE)`, and the spread
between the best and worst rules is smaller than the difference between paying
an 8-to-18% over-round and paying 2-to-5% commission.

The fair-book column makes the same point from the other side. Three rules in
the shortlist are profitable with the margin removed and none is profitable
with it in place. Changing the venue does not create an edge. It changes how
much edge a rule needs before one survives.

## Two things this dataset cannot answer

**Is real money available at early prices, in usable size?** Everything above
assumes the bet can be struck. The Smartform archive records what prices
existed, not what money stood behind them. Early exchange markets on UK
All-Weather handicaps are thin. A price available for one unit may not be
available for fifty, and a price that moves when you bet into it is not the
price you modelled. If the available size is small enough, the edge is real
and unusable, which is the same thing operationally as not having it.

**Does the model beat an early exchange price?** Paper 4's result is against
`daily_runners.forecast_price_decimal`, a forecast published the evening
before by a compiler. That is not a price money has traded at. An early
exchange price aggregates the opinions of people who have committed funds, and
it will already contain much of what a compiler's forecast misses. Beating a
forecast price is weak evidence of beating an early traded price. This dataset
contains no early traded prices, so the gap cannot be measured here.

Neither question is a footnote. They decide whether any of this works, and
answering them needs a live feed and paper trading, not another backtest on
this archive.

## A correction to the series

Two of the four markets reported throughout papers 2b to 6 price bets that do
not quite exist on the venue this strategy would use.

**Betfair has no each-way market.** An each-way bet is a bookmaker product:
one stake on the win, one on a place at a fraction of the odds. On an exchange
those are two separate markets and the each-way construction has no
counterpart. Every each-way figure in papers 2b, 5 and 6, at paper 5's flat
one-fifth top-three terms and at the corrected industry ladder alike, prices
something that cannot be placed there.

**Betfair's place market is independently priced.** The place prices in this
series are not. They are a discounted-Harville construction computed from the
win prices, following @harville1973 with the @lobaconshone1994 corrections.
That was the right choice for papers 2b to 5, because it makes the place
market comparable to the win market on the same information. It is not the
price a place bet would be struck at, and a real place market can disagree
with anything derived from win prices.

Of the four markets in this paper, win is real and priced as traded, place is
real but priced here by proxy, and the two each-way columns are products of a
different venue. The win numbers are the ones that carry forward.
